lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Thank you for listening. Are there any questions? Dr. Vale and Lumi wave goodbye at the door, and I lead everyone along a path of glowing pages. Soon, we step into a huge maze. The walls are tall bookshelves and hedges with paper leaves. Warm lanterns glimmer everywhere, and signposts show story titles. Then a small gray mouse in a red cape runs up to us. He is carrying a feather pen and a heavy old book. He bows and says, Welcome to the Labyrinth of Tales! I'm Nib, your guide. Every path in this maze tells a story. Say it with me. Every path in this maze tells a story. Great! Nib opens his book. It's the Storybook of the Labyrinth, and its last six pages are completely blank. Let's read the note on the first page. "Welcome, travelers! This is the Labyrinth of Tales. Its walls are made of bookshelves and hedges, and every path leads to a room where a story lives. In the middle of the maze is the Central Hall, where the Storytelling Festival will be held. This Storybook is very old, but it isn't finished yet. Its last six pages are still blank. They are waiting for friends who can learn the six secrets of stories. Each time you learn a secret, one blank page will fill with shining words. When all six pages are full, the Storybook will be complete. Please stay together, follow the lanterns, and listen carefully. And then what happened? That part is up to you!" Where will the Storytelling Festival be held? In the Central Hall. How many pages are still blank? Six. Far away, an old voice is telling a story. Nib says, That's Granny Willa. She sits by the fire in the Hearth Room. You'll meet her one day. Then he asks his favorite question, And then what happened? That's his catchphrase! Now, phonics. Strong verbs show how something happens. Whisper means to speak very quietly, using your breath. Whisper begins with w-h, but it sounds like w. Glimmer means to shine with a weak light that comes and goes. Tremble means to shake a little because you are scared, cold or excited. Tremble ends in b, l, e, and that part sounds like bull. Next time, we'll visit the first room and meet a very clever rabbit!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Every path in this maze tells a story. Today, Nib and I lead everyone down a path with a signpost that says The Clever Rabbit. At the end, there is a cozy room with a round green door. Inside, the walls are painted with tall grass and a big orange sunset. Nib jumps onto a stool, opens the Storybook and says, Many countries have stories about clever animals. Here is one from the Labyrinth. Listen carefully! It's about a tiny rabbit and a big, hungry tiger. The tiger is much stronger, but the rabbit has something better: a plan. The rabbit tricked the tiger with a smart idea. Say it with me. The rabbit tricked the tiger with a smart idea. Great! Let's read the story page. "Once upon a time, a little rabbit was hopping home with a basket of carrots. Suddenly, a big tiger stepped onto the path. He was hungry, and he was very grumpy. Give me those carrots, he growled. The rabbit's legs began to tremble, but she thought fast. Oh, these are magic carrots, she said. They only taste sweet if you close your eyes and count to one thousand. The tiger wanted the sweetest carrots in the world, so he closed his eyes. One, two, three... While the tiger was counting, the rabbit hopped quietly home. When the tiger reached one thousand, he opened his eyes. The rabbit was gone! At first, he was angry. Then he started to laugh. What a clever trick! he said. The next day, he knocked on the rabbit's door and asked nicely. So she shared her carrots with him." Why did the tiger close his eyes? Because he wanted the carrots to taste sweet. What did the tiger learn? He learned to ask nicely. Haru gasps and says, Count to one thousand? That would take forever! Birimo tries it and gives up at twelve. Nib smiles and asks, And then what happened? Now, phonics. Gasp means to breathe in quickly because you are surprised. Haru gasped when he heard the trick. Stumble means to almost fall while you are walking. Stumble ends in l-e, just like tremble. Glance means to look very quickly. When the tiger opened his eyes, he glanced around, but the rabbit was gone! Next time, we'll find out why the moon seems to change its shape.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The rabbit tricked the tiger with a smart idea. Today, Nib takes us to a dark blue room with a silver ceiling. Tiny stars sparkle above us, and a big, round moon lamp hangs in the middle. This is the Moon Room, Nib whispers. Long ago, people looked up at the night sky and wondered. Why is the moon round one week and thin the next? So they made up stories. Long ago, people told stories to explain the moon. Say it with me. Long ago, people told stories to explain the moon. Great! Let's read the old tale on the wall. "Why the Moon Changes. Long ago, people said that the moon was the kindest light in the sky. Every night, it watched over the sleepy animals below. Some of them were afraid of the dark. The little rabbits would shiver in their holes, and the baby deer couldn't sleep. So the moon broke off a piece of its own light and gave it to them. The next night, it gave away another piece, and then another. Little by little, the moon became thinner, until it was only a thin silver smile. Then, slowly, its light grew back, night after night, until it was round and bright again. And every month, the kind moon gives its light away once more." Why did the moon give away its light? Because some animals were afraid of the dark. What happened to the moon after that? It became thinner, and then it grew back. Riko says, That's a beautiful story. But what's the real reason? I smile and explain. The moon doesn't really change shape. The sun always lights half of it. As the moon travels around the Earth, we see different amounts of that bright half. Sometimes we see all of it, and we call it a full moon. Sometimes we see only a thin crescent. One cycle takes about a month, about 29 and a half days. Nib claps his tiny paws. A true reason and a kind story. I like both! Now, phonics. Shiver means to shake because you are cold. Sparkle means to shine with many tiny flashes of light. Sparkle ends in l-e. Wander means to walk slowly with no special place to go. Next time, we'll visit a great hall full of stories from many lands.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Long ago, people told stories to explain the moon. Today, Nib leads us into the Hall of Many Lands. It is the biggest room we have seen so far. There are hundreds of shelves, and each shelf holds books from a different part of the world. Paper birds flutter above our heads. Nib climbs a ladder and says, Here's a secret. Stories from faraway places are often alike! Haru looks at the books on the shelves. Many of them are about children who do something brave to help their families. Many countries have stories about brave children. Say it with me. Many countries have stories about brave children. Great! Let's read the sign at the entrance of the hall. "Welcome to the Hall of Many Lands! People all over the world tell stories and legends, and many of them follow the same patterns. Here are five patterns you can find on these shelves. First, a brave child goes somewhere difficult to help a family or a village. Second, something happens three times, and the third time is special. For example, a girl knocks on three doors, and only the third one opens. Third, a small animal beats a big one by using its brain. Fourth, a magic object, such as a spoon that never runs out of soup, changes everything. Fifth, a hero goes on a long journey and comes home wiser. Look for these patterns as you read. You will be surprised how often you find them!" How many patterns are on the sign? Five. What happens when the girl knocks on three doors? Only the third one opens. Kiko says, The clever rabbit is the third pattern! A small animal beats a big one. Birimo grins and says, A spoon that never runs out of soup? I want one! Riko mutters with a smile, Birimo, you're always thinking about food. Everyone laughs, and Nib asks, And then what happened? Now, phonics. Grin means to smile a big smile that shows your teeth. Mutter means to say something quietly, often when you are not happy. Flutter means to move up and down quickly and lightly, the way a butterfly's wings move. Mutter and flutter both have a double t after a short u sound. Next time, we'll talk about the lessons that stories teach us.

He says, Every story has a little gift inside it. We call it the lesson. Let's find the lessons together. First, Nib reads a short tale from the Storybook. It's about a small bird who tries again and again. When he finishes, Riko says, The lesson of this story is: Don't give up. Say it with me. The lesson of this story is: Don't give up. Great! Let's read the tale. "The Little Builder. Once upon a time, a little bird named Pip wanted to build a nest at the top of the tallest tree. The other birds laughed. It's too windy up there! they said. Pip built her first nest with dry grass, but the wind blew it away. She built a second nest with leaves, but the rain washed it down. Pip felt like crying, but she didn't stop. For her third nest, she wove grass, leaves and soft mud together very tightly. That night, a big storm came. In the morning, the other birds looked up. Pip's nest was still there, and Pip was singing in it. Soon, all the birds wanted to learn how to build a nest like hers." How many nests did Pip build? Three. Why did the third nest stay? Because she wove grass, leaves and mud together tightly. Then we remember other stories. The lesson of the rabbit story is: Brains beat strength. In the Hall of Many Lands, a tired girl knocked on three doors, and a kind woman opened the third one. That lesson is: Be kind to strangers. Suddenly, the Storybook begins to sparkle. One blank page fills with shining words. It's the first golden page! Nib whispers, The first secret of stories: every story carries a lesson. Now, phonics. Let's review. Whisper means to speak very quietly. It begins with w-h, but it sounds like w. Gasp means to breathe in quickly because you are surprised. We all gasped when the page began to shine! Sparkle means to shine with many tiny flashes of light, and it ends in l-e. Next time, we'll visit Nib's Story Workshop and learn how stories are built.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The lesson of this story is: Don't give up. Today, Nib takes us to his Story Workshop. It's a busy room full of wooden drawers. They are labeled SETTING, CHARACTERS, PROBLEM and WORDS. Pencils and paper are everywhere, and a pan of pancakes is sizzling on a little stove in the corner. Birimo's eyes light up. Nib laughs and says, Snacks later! First, every story needs three things. Where and when does it happen? That's the setting. Who is in it? Those are the characters. What goes wrong? That's the problem. Today's story is called The Frozen Kingdom. The story takes place in a frozen kingdom. Say it with me. The story takes place in a frozen kingdom. Great! Let's read the first page. "The Frozen Kingdom. Long ago, in a kingdom high in the mountains, the Sun Bird lived on the tallest tower of the palace. Every morning, she spread her golden feathers, and the whole kingdom felt warm. One winter night, a wild wind blew, and her golden feathers flew away over the mountains. The next morning, the sun gave no warmth. Snow fell off the roofs with a thud. The river turned to ice, and the people stayed inside by their fires. Oren, a young shepherd boy, looked at his sheep. They were shivering in the snow. Someone has to find those feathers, he said. His grandmother put on her warmest coat. Then I'm coming with you, she said. So together, they packed some bread and started walking toward the mountains." Where does the story take place? In a frozen kingdom in the mountains. What is the problem? The Sun Bird lost her golden feathers, so everything froze. Kiko opens the CHARACTERS drawer and finds three cards: Oren, his grandmother and the Sun Bird. Nib asks, And then what happened? We'll find out soon! Now, phonics. Sound words sound like the noise they describe. Thud is the sound of something heavy falling on a soft place, like snow falling off a roof. Rustle is the sound of dry leaves moving. Sizzle is the sound of food cooking in a hot pan, like Nib's pancakes. Next time, we'll learn how to show feelings without saying them.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The story takes place in a frozen kingdom. Today, Nib opens the drawer marked WORDS. Inside, there is a card with one big sentence: Show, don't tell（見せて つたえる）. Nib explains. If you write, Oren was scared, you tell the reader. But if you write about his body, the reader can see it and feel it. Kiko tries a sentence about a scared girl. Her hands were shaking. Nib cheers. That's it! You didn't say scared, but we know! Her hands were shaking. Say it with me. Her hands were shaking. Great! Let's read two versions of the next part of The Frozen Kingdom. "Version A: Oren was scared and cold. His grandmother was worried. Version B: Oren stood at the bottom of the icy mountain. His hands were shaking, and his teeth chattered. Above him, the path disappeared into the clouds. His grandmother pulled her scarf tighter. She didn't say anything, but she held his hand a little more firmly. Then a small sound came from under the snow: drip, drip, drip. Oren knelt down. Under the ice, a tiny stream of water was still moving. Oren took a deep breath and smiled for the first time that day. Maybe, he whispered, the kingdom isn't completely frozen yet." Which version is more exciting? Version B. How do we know Oren is scared? His hands were shaking, and his teeth chattered. How do we know his grandmother is worried? She held his hand more firmly. Haru frowns and thinks. Then he says, Version A is short, but Version B puts a picture in my head. Birimo pretends to shiver and makes his teeth chatter very loudly. Nib asks, And then what happened? Now, phonics. Here are more sound words. Drip is the sound of water falling one drop at a time, like the water under the ice. Boom is a loud, deep sound, like fireworks or thunder. Crackle is the sound of a campfire, with many little snaps. Next time, Oren will need to be very brave, and we'll learn a new way to describe him.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Her hands were shaking. Today, there's a loud clang in the Story Workshop. Birimo has knocked over a pile of metal cookie tins! Nib laughs and helps him pick them up. Then he opens a new drawer. Inside, there are cards with animals on them. Nib says, When we compare one thing to another using as or like, it's called a simile. A simile puts a picture in the reader's head. Oren is about to do something very brave. We could just say he was brave. But it's more fun to say this. He was as brave as a lion. Say it with me. He was as brave as a lion. Great! Let's read the next page of The Frozen Kingdom. "Oren and his grandmother climbed higher and higher. The wind was as cold as ice. At the top of the mountain, they found an ice cave. Inside, the walls shone like glass, and there, in a pile of snow, lay the golden feathers. Suddenly, a huge white snake slid out and hissed. Oren's knees were shaking, but he didn't run. He was as brave as a lion. Excuse me, he said politely. We need those feathers to warm our kingdom. The snake blinked in surprise. Nobody has ever said excuse me to me, it said. Then it pushed the feathers toward him with its nose. Just at that moment, there was a whoosh, and a golden shape flew across the sky like a shooting star. It was the Sun Bird!" How was Oren brave? He didn't run, and he spoke politely to the snake. How did the Sun Bird fly? Like a shooting star. Riko says, I love the snake. It wasn't mean. It just needed someone to be polite. Nib nods and asks, And then what happened? Now, phonics. More sound words! Hiss is the sound a snake makes, or the sound of steam. Whoosh is the sound of something rushing past very fast, like the Sun Bird. Clang is the sound of metal hitting metal, like Birimo's cookie tins. Next time, we'll walk down a very noisy corridor.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, He was as brave as a lion. Today, Nib leads us down the Creaking Corridor. It's long and narrow, and candles flicker on the walls. Every floorboard creaks under our feet, and our footsteps echo. Kiko holds my hand. At the end, there is a tall wooden door. Nib grins and pushes it. Creak! The old door slowly opened. Say it with me. Creak! The old door slowly opened. Great! Behind the door, there is no monster at all, just Nib's sleepy cat, Button, yawning in a basket. Everyone laughs. Nib says, Sound words make a scene come alive. Let's read the last page of The Frozen Kingdom. "The Sun Bird landed on Oren's arm, and her feathers glowed. Together, Oren and his grandmother walked down the mountain, and the Sun Bird flew above them. When they reached the kingdom, she spread her golden wings. Crash! The thick ice on the river broke into pieces. Splash! The water began to run again, and the fish jumped for joy. Drip, drip, drip went the icicles on every roof. Then Oren knocked on the palace door. Creak! The old door slowly opened, and the queen stepped out into the warm sunshine. Thank you, Oren, she said with a smile. From that day on, the Sun Bird kept her feathers safe, and every spring, the people held a festival of golden kites." What happened to the ice on the river? It broke into pieces. Who opened the palace door? The queen. Haru says, I liked the ending, because everyone was happy and the sheep were warm again. Riko asks, Did the snake come to the festival too? Nib laughs. That's a great question! And then what happened? You can decide! Now, phonics. Crash is the loud sound of something breaking or falling, like the ice on the river. Splash is the sound of something falling into water. Crash and splash both end in a-s-h. Creak is the sound of an old door or floor. Next time, it's the Story Lab, and each of you will read your own short paragraph!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Creak! The old door slowly opened. Today is the Story Lab. Nib has turned his workshop into a little laboratory. There are glass jars on every shelf, and each jar is filled with words: sound words, similes and showing words. Nib says, Today, each of you will read a short description of a place. Use everything you've learned! Kiko goes first. Her paragraph is about a snowy forest. Her best sentence is this one. The forest was so quiet that she could hear her heartbeat. Say it with me. The forest was so quiet that she could hear her heartbeat. Great! Let's read Kiko's paragraph. "The Snowy Forest. Just after sunset, a girl and her grandfather walked into the forest. Snow covered every branch, and the moon peeked through the trees. The forest was so quiet that she could hear her heartbeat. The snow under her boots was as soft as a pillow. Her breath made little clouds in the air. She began to shiver, and she pulled her red scarf up to her nose. Suddenly, there was a crash behind her. She turned around slowly. A pile of snow had fallen from a tall pine tree. On top of it sat a tiny owl, blinking its big yellow eyes. The girl laughed so loudly that the owl flew away, and her grandfather laughed, too." What made the crash? A pile of snow fell from a pine tree. What was sitting on the snow? A tiny owl. Then Haru reads about a windy beach, and Riko reads about an old house where every door creaks. Birimo reads about a snowman who sneezed so hard that his carrot nose flew across the room. Everyone claps and laughs. Suddenly, the Storybook glows. A blank page fills with shining words. It's the second golden page! Nib reads it aloud. The second secret of stories: paint pictures with your words. Now, phonics. Let's review. Crash is the sound of something breaking or falling. Creak is the sound of an old door or floor. Shiver means to shake because you are cold. Next time, we'll meet a very old and very gentle golden dragon.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, The forest was so quiet that she could hear her heartbeat. Today, Nib takes us down a new path in the Labyrinth. I walk at the front with a lantern, and we all stay close together. At the end of the path, there is a round room full of soft golden light. In the middle, on a pile of old cushions, lies a huge dragon. Her scales are gold, and her eyes are kind and sleepy. This is Saffron, and she is very old. Saffron smiles and says, Welcome, little travelers. Now my wings are tired, so I stay here and tell riddles. Kiko looks at Saffron's tired wings and says softly, If I were a dragon, I would fly over the ocean. Say it with me. If I were a dragon, I would fly over the ocean. Great! We say If I were ～ when we imagine something that isn't true. Let's read the riddle card on Saffron's wall. "Saffron's Riddle Room. Welcome, travelers! Long ago, I flew across the whole world. I saw seven seas, and I counted the stars over every one of them. Now my wings are old, but my mind is still young, so I love riddles. Here is today's riddle. I have pages, but I am not a tree. I have a spine, but I am not an animal. I can take you anywhere, but I have no legs. What am I? When you know the answer, tell me. Then tell me this: If you were a dragon, where would you fly? I will tell you a story about that place. Your friend, Saffron" Why does Saffron stay in the Dragon Room now? Because her wings are old and tired. What is the answer to the riddle? A book! Haru shouts it first, and Saffron's tail thumps happily on the floor. Now, phonics. When we tell a story aloud, we lower our voice and pause just before the surprise. She opened the box, and inside was, pause, a tiny dragon! The footsteps came closer and closer, and then, pause, they stopped. He looked up, and there in the tree sat, pause, a giant owl. Behind the curtain stood, pause, a little gray mouse. But never pause in the middle of a group like a tiny dragon! Next time, Saffron will show us a secret well that listens to wishes.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, If I were a dragon, I would fly over the ocean. Today, Saffron shows us a small door behind her cushions. I go first, and everyone follows me down some stone steps into a quiet garden. In the middle of the garden is an old stone well covered in moss. When Nib leans over the edge, the water bubbles, and a voice comes up. It sounds like a happy kettle! Blub, blub! Welcome to the Well of Wishes! The well doesn't want coins. It wants kind wishes, and you have to say them out loud. Birimo goes first. He says, I wish I could eat pancakes for breakfast forever! The water gives a little giggle. Then Kiko sees a bird on the edge of the well and says, I wish I could talk to animals. Say it with me. I wish I could talk to animals. Great! We say I wish I could ～ when we want to do something, but we can't do it now. Let's read the sign next to the well. "The Well of Wishes. Hello, traveler! I am a very old well, and I have heard thousands of wishes. Some were big, and some were small. Here are my three rules. First, say your wish out loud and clearly. I am a little hard of hearing! Second, make it a kind wish. Unkind wishes turn into mud, and nobody likes mud. Third, a wish is not a magic trick. If you wish you could swim, the best way is to practice. I will cheer for you! When a kind wish touches my water, it sparkles. Come closer, and let's see what happens. Blub, blub!" What does the well want instead of coins? Kind wishes, said out loud. What happens when a kind wish touches the water? It sparkles. When Kiko says her wish, the water sparkles like a thousand tiny stars, and the bird sings a little song. Now, phonics. Let's pause before the surprise again. The cave was dark and silent, until suddenly, pause, a voice said hello. At the bottom of the well, she found, pause, a golden key. The thing under the bed was not a monster, pause, but a puppy. When the clock struck twelve, the statue, pause, opened its eyes. Next time, Nib will teach us a question game with a magic key!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I wish I could talk to animals. Today, Nib leads us to a big round table. On the table, there are three boxes with pictures of a key, a cape and a door. Nib jumps onto the table, swishes his red cape and says, Welcome to my favorite game! It's called What Would You Do? You pick a card, and you answer the question. There are no wrong answers, but you must give a reason. Haru picks the first card. What would you do if you found a magic key? Say it with me. What would you do if you found a magic key? Great! We use it to imagine something that probably won't happen. To answer, say If I found ～, I would ～. Let's read Nib's game cards. "Nib's Game: What Would You Do? Card One. What would you do if you found a magic key? It can open any door in the world, but only once. Which door would you choose, and why? Card Two. What would you do if you had an invisible cape? You can wear it for one day. Where would you go? Remember, a good hero uses it kindly! Card Three. What would you do if you found a door to anywhere? Bonus Card. What would you do if you met a friendly dragon who couldn't fly? Rules: Listen to each answer. Then ask one more question, like Why? or And then what happened? Have fun!" How many times can the magic key open a door? Only once. What should you do after each answer? Ask one more question. Haru says, If I found a magic key, I would open the door to the oldest room in the maze, because I want to read the very first story. Birimo picks the Bonus Card and says, I would give Saffron a ride on my back! Everyone laughs, because Birimo is tiny. Now, phonics. Pause before the surprise. She lifted the lid very slowly and saw, pause, a pair of eyes. Out of the giant egg came, pause, a baby star. The last door opened, and in the room was, pause, the dragon queen. The rabbit lifted the cup, and under it sat, pause, a frog. Remember, don't pause in the middle of a group like a baby star. Next time, we'll meet a girl from the mountains with a big dream.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What would you do if you found a magic key? Today, Nib takes us to a small blue room. It smells like salt, and we can hear soft waves somewhere. On a shelf, there is a big pink seashell next to a pair of tiny hiking boots. Nib says, These belonged to Pell. Sit down, and I'll tell you her story. We all sit together on a soft rug. Pell lived in a village high in the mountains. She had seen snow, rivers and eagles, but she had never seen the sea before. Say it with me. She had never seen the sea before. Great! Had never seen（いちども 見た ことが なかった） means not even once, up until that time in the story. Let's read the page about Pell. "Pell lived in a village so high in the mountains that clouds floated through the streets. Every evening, her grandmother held a pink seashell to Pell's ear. Listen, she said. That is the sound of the sea. Pell had never seen the sea, but she dreamed about it every night. One spring, a kind traveling baker offered to take Pell and her grandmother down the mountain in his wagon. They traveled for seven days. The air got warmer, and the trees changed. On the last morning, Pell smelled something salty. She climbed to the top of a sandy hill, and she gasped. She had never seen the sea before, and now it was right in front of her, wide and blue and shining. She held up the shell. It sang the same song." Who traveled with Pell? Her grandmother and a kind baker. What did Pell smell on the last morning? Something salty. Kiko says quietly, The shell and the sea sang the same song. That's my favorite part. Nib wipes a happy tear with his cape and says, And then what happened? Pell built a sandcastle, of course! Now, phonics. Let's pause just before the big moment. She had never seen the sea before, and now, pause, it was right in front of her. Little by little, the fog cleared, and they saw, pause, the castle. He reached into his pocket and pulled out, pause, a glowing stone. The voice in the dark whispered one word, pause, welcome. Next time, we'll talk about three wishes!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, She had never seen the sea before. Today, we go back to the Dragon Room, because Saffron has a surprise. The Well of Wishes has sent a little stream of bubbly water up into a stone bowl next to her cushions. Saffron says, In many old stories, someone gets three wishes. Let's play. Tell me your three wishes, but remember, at least one of them must help other people. Riko goes first and says, If I had three wishes, I would ask for a flying bike, a library in my room and a sunny day for everyone. Say it with me. If I had three wishes, I would ask for a flying bike, a library in my room and a sunny day for everyone. Great! Riko's third wish helps everyone. Let's read the wish list that Nib wrote with his feather pen. "Our Three Wishes, by Nib. Riko wishes for a flying bike, a library in her room and a sunny day for everyone, so that nobody's picnic gets rained on. Haru wishes for a telescope that can see other planets, a robot that cleans his room and a big park for every town, where children and grandparents can play together. Kiko wishes she could talk to animals, of course! Her other wishes are a warm bed for every stray cat and a tree house in the clouds. Birimo wishes for pancakes forever, pancakes for his friends forever and, after thinking hard, a new pair of strong wings for Saffron. Saffron read the list twice and smiled. Then her golden eyes got a little wet." Which of Haru's wishes helps other people? A big park for every town. What was Birimo's last wish? New wings for Saffron. Saffron stretches her old wings and laughs softly. She says, That is the kindest wish I have heard in a hundred years. At that moment, the Storybook begins to glow. Nib opens it, and the third golden page appears, full of shining words. Nib reads it aloud. The third secret of stories: a wish is strongest when it is shared. Now, phonics. Let's review. She opened the box, and inside was, pause, a tiny dragon! Splash is the sound of something falling into water. Whisper starts with a w sound, and it means to speak very quietly, using your breath. Next time, we'll start planning our very own stories!

Nib says, You've heard lots of stories in the Labyrinth. Now it's time to plan your own! Haru writes The Boy and the Stone Giant. Riko writes The Lighthouse Cat. Birimo writes The Dragon Who Sneezed Glitter. Kiko smiles and writes in the HERO box. My hero is a girl who can talk to the wind. Say it with me. My hero is a girl who can talk to the wind. Great! A hero is the main character of a story. Let's read Kiko's story map. "Story Map by Kiko. Title: The Girl Who Talked to the Wind. Hero: My hero is a girl named Aria who can talk to the wind. She is curious and kind, but sometimes she doesn't listen carefully. Place: Aria lives in a village above the clouds with her parents and her little brother. The wind visits her every evening and tells her about faraway lands. Problem: One night, a strange wind carries Aria far away from home. Now she is in a land she doesn't know, and she can't find the way back. Questions to think about: Who will help her? What will she learn? How will she get home? Nib's note: Great plan, Kiko! A hero with a small weakness is more interesting." What is Aria's weakness? Sometimes she doesn't listen carefully. What is her problem? A strange wind carries her far away, and she can't find the way back. Haru's hero is a boy named Leo who finds a sleepy stone giant on a mountain path. Riko's hero is a cat named Pepper who lives in an old lighthouse. Birimo's hero is a young dragon named Fizz who sneezes glitter instead of fire. Now, phonics. Words that end in l y tell us how a character does something. Suddenly, the wind blew. She opened the door carefully. He walked bravely into the cave. To make these words, we usually just add l y. Sudden becomes suddenly, careful becomes carefully, and brave becomes bravely. Next time, we'll learn how to write a first line that grabs the reader.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My hero is a girl who can talk to the wind. Today, Nib pulls open a drawer labeled BEGINNINGS. Inside, there are hundreds of tiny paper cards, and each card has the first line of a story. Nib says, The first line is like a door. If it opens in an exciting way, readers want to come in! I read Kiko's first try out loud. Once there was a girl named Aria. She was nice. Kiko frowns and says, It's true, but it's a bit boring. Then she writes a new line. On the coldest night of the year, a strange wind knocked on her window. Say it with me. On the coldest night of the year, a strange wind knocked on her window. Great! Now we want to know who is knocking and why. Let's read Nib's workshop card. "Nib's Workshop Card: Strong Beginnings. A strong beginning makes the reader ask a question. Here are two beginnings of the same story. Beginning A: Once there was a girl named Aria. She lived above the clouds. She was nice. Beginning B: On the coldest night of the year, a strange wind knocked on her window. Aria sat up in bed. The wind had never knocked before. Beginning A gives us facts, but nothing happens. Beginning B starts with a surprise, so we want to read more. Try these tricks. Start with a sound. Start with something strange. Start with a question, like Who would knock on a window at midnight? Then ask yourself: Would I turn the page?" Why is Beginning B stronger? It starts with a surprise, so we want to read more. What is one trick for a strong beginning? Start with a sound, something strange or a question. Riko writes, On a stormy night, Pepper the lighthouse cat could not sleep. Birimo's first line is just one word. Achoo! Nib laughs and says, That's a sound, so it counts! Now, phonics. The cat crept silently down the stairs. Aria nervously opened the window. The wind gently touched her face. Silent becomes silently. Nervous becomes nervously. Gentle is a little different: we take away the e and add y, so it becomes gently. Next time, we'll find the moment in our stories where everything changes.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, On the coldest night of the year, a strange wind knocked on her window. Today, Nib draws a big hill on the blackboard in the Story Workshop. At the bottom of one side, he writes BEGINNING. At the top, he writes TURNING POINT. At the bottom of the other side, he writes ENDING. He says, A story is like climbing a hill. At the top, something happens that changes everything. That's the turning point! I ask, What's the turning point in Pell's story? Riko answers, When she sees the sea! Exactly. Now Kiko needs a turning point for Aria. The strange wind has carried Aria to a land of dry deserts and tall mountains, and she is lost and tired. Kiko writes, Just then, she heard a voice behind her. Say it with me. Just then, she heard a voice behind her. Great! Just then means at that exact moment. Let's read Kiko's middle page. "Aria walked and walked across the dry sand. Everything was silent. She called the wind's name, but nobody answered. Her feet were tired, and she missed her little brother. She sat down on a rock and hugged her knees. Just then, she heard a voice behind her. It was quiet and a little shy. Excuse me, it said. Are you the girl who talks to the wind? Aria turned around slowly. There, floating in the air, was a tiny breeze, no bigger than a kitten. I'm the youngest wind, it said, and I'm the one who carried you here. I'm sorry. I got lost, and I needed a friend who could listen." How did Aria feel before the turning point? Tired, and she missed her little brother. Who was talking behind her? The youngest wind. Birimo shouts, No way! The wind was the problem and the friend! Nib grins and says, And then what happened? You'll find out in the next chapter! Haru's turning point is when the stone giant opens his eyes and says, Please don't go. Riko's is when the cat sees a little boat lost in the fog. Now, phonics. The stone giant stood up proudly. The cat eagerly ran up the stairs. Outside, the wind blew fiercely. Proud becomes proudly. Eager becomes eagerly. Fierce becomes fiercely: we keep the e and add l y. Next time, we'll learn how to give our stories a happy, satisfying ending.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Just then, she heard a voice behind her. Today, Nib points to the other side of the hill on his blackboard, the side that goes down to the ENDING. He says, A good ending does two things. It solves the problem, and it shows how the hero has changed. I add, And it should feel just right, like the last piece of a puzzle. So what does Aria learn? At the beginning, she didn't always listen carefully. So in the ending, she listens. She hears that the little wind is lonely, and she becomes its friend. Then Kiko writes her last line. In the end, the wind carried her home. Say it with me. In the end, the wind carried her home. Great! In the end means finally, after everything that happened. Let's read Kiko's last page. "Aria listened to the youngest wind for a long time. It told her about the places it had seen and how lonely it felt, because the big winds were always too busy to play. I can be your friend, Aria said, but my family will be worried. Can you take me home? The little wind thought for a moment. Then it blew softly, and Aria rose into the air, as light as a dandelion seed. They flew over deserts, rivers and sleeping towns, up to her village. In the end, the wind carried her home. Every evening after that, a small breeze tapped on her window, and Aria always opened it to listen." Why was the youngest wind lonely? Because the big winds were always too busy to play. How does Aria change? She learns to listen carefully. Riko says, That's such a satisfying ending. Haru's story ends with the stone giant waving to travelers on the mountain path. In Riko's story, the cat lights the lamp, and the little boat gets home safely. In Birimo's story, the king loves the glitter so much that he holds a Sparkle Festival every year. Nib says, And then what happened? Nothing! That's how you know it's the end! Now, phonics. The boat finally reached the harbor. The giant looked curiously at the boy. The dragon danced gracefully in the sky. Final becomes finally. Curious becomes curiously. Graceful becomes gracefully, just like careful and carefully. Next time is Lesson 1100, and Nib says there will be a party!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, In the end, the wind carried her home. Today is a very special day. It's our 1,100th lesson! When we walk into the Story Workshop, we all gasp. The room is full of paper lanterns, and each lantern is folded from a page of an old story. On the big table, there is a tall cake shaped like a stack of books, with a tiny chocolate mouse on top. I light the candles. Saffron has sent a basket of warm cinnamon rolls from the Dragon Room, and the Well of Wishes has sent a big bottle of bubbly lemonade. Nib climbs onto a teacup and shouts, Let's share our story ideas! Say it with me. Let's share our story ideas! Great! Let's read the party program. "The Story Idea Party! Program. One: Cake and lemonade. Nib asks you to save the chocolate mouse for him. Two: Story Idea Share. Each friend tells the title, the hero and the problem of their story in one minute. Kiko: The Girl Who Talked to the Wind. Riko: The Lighthouse Cat. Haru: The Boy and the Stone Giant. Birimo: The Dragon Who Sneezed Glitter. Three: Friendly Questions. After each idea, ask one question, like Who helps the hero? or What happens next? Four: Lantern Wishes. Write one kind wish for your story on a paper lantern. Please clap loudly and laugh kindly. Thank you for being such brave and creative storytellers!" What does each friend tell in one minute? The title, the hero and the problem of their story. What do the friends write on the paper lanterns? One kind wish for their story. The friends share their ideas bravely, and everyone claps. When Birimo shouts Achoo, the whole room laughs. Then the Storybook begins to glow, and the fourth golden page appears! It says, The fourth secret of stories: every story begins with one small idea. Far away in the maze, we hear an old voice telling a story by a crackling fire. Now, phonics. Let's review. Bravely means in a brave way: brave plus l y. At the bottom of the well, she found, pause, a golden key. Boom is the sound of fireworks or thunder. Glimmer means to shine with a weak light that comes and goes, just like our paper lanterns. Next time, we'll meet Granny Willa, the old storyteller in the Hearth Room!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Let's share our story ideas! After the party, Nib leads us down a warm, narrow path. At the end of the path, there is a round wooden door. Nib knocks three times and says, This is the Hearth Room. Someone very special lives here. Inside, a fire is crackling in a big stone fireplace. In a rocking chair sits an old woman with a patchwork shawl and kind, twinkling eyes. It's Granny Willa! We heard her voice at the beginning of the Labyrinth. She smiles and says, Come in, my dears. Sit close to the fire. Writing a story is one thing. Telling it out loud is another. Then she teaches us her favorite trick. First, stop talking for a moment. Next, speak quietly so everyone leans in. Then, surprise them! Say it with me. Pause. Lower your voice. Then, BOO! Great! Birimo jumps so high that his cushion flies across the room. Let's read Granny Willa's storytelling card. "Granny Willa's Three Secrets for Telling a Story Aloud. One: Slow down. When you are excited, you talk fast, but your listeners need time to see the pictures in their heads. Two: Change your voice. Use a big, deep voice for a giant and a tiny, squeaky voice for a mouse. When something is mysterious, speak more and more softly. Three: Pause before the surprise. Stop for one, two, three seconds. Look at your listeners. Let them wait and wonder. Then say the surprise clearly, with a big smile. Remember, a story is not just words on a page. It is a gift that you give with your voice, your face and your hands. Practice in front of a friend, and don't worry about mistakes. Every storyteller makes them!" Why should we slow down? Because our listeners need time to see the pictures in their heads. When should we pause? Right before the surprise. Haru tries it. He speaks softly, The box began to shake, and out jumped... BOO! Everyone laughs, even Granny Willa. Now, phonics. A simile compares two things with as and as. The knight was as brave as a lion. During the spooky part, the room was as quiet as a mouse. And Granny Willa is as busy as a bee, because she knits a scarf while she tells stories! Next time, we'll learn how to talk to our audience.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Pause. Lower your voice. Then, BOO! Today, the fire in the Hearth Room is glowing orange, and Granny Willa is knitting a long purple scarf. She looks up and says, A story is like a game of catch. You throw it to your listeners, and they throw something back. Then she shows us how. She looks right into our eyes, she asks us questions, and she lets us guess. Nib loves this. He sits on the arm of her chair with his feather pen and keeps whispering, And then what happened? Granny Willa has a favorite question. Just before the surprise, she stops and asks the audience, Can you guess what happened next? Say it with me. Can you guess what happened next? Wonderful! When the listeners guess, they feel like part of the story. Let's read Granny Willa's story about a very small hero. "The Little Snail and the Snow Lantern. Long ago, on a mountain where the wind was as cold as ice, there lived a little snail named Dot. Every winter, the animals lit a big lantern on top of the mountain, so travelers could find their way through the snow. But one night, the lantern went out. Who do you think climbed up to light it again? The strong bear? The fast deer? No! They were all fast asleep. Only Dot was awake. She was, of course, very slow, but she never stopped climbing. Up, up, up she went, all night long. When the sun came up, she finally reached the top. Can you guess what happened next? She breathed one warm breath on the lantern, and it began to glow! The travelers below cheered for the smallest climber on the mountain." Why did Dot climb the mountain? Because the lantern went out and the other animals were asleep. What made the lantern glow? Dot's warm breath. Riko says, I guessed the bear! Granny Willa laughs. That's the fun of it, my dear. A good guess, and a happy surprise. Now, phonics. Here are more similes with as and as. The wind on the mountain was as cold as ice. A snowflake is as light as a feather. And Dot was as slow as a snail, because she was a snail! Which word goes in as light as a ... ? Feather! Next time, we'll give our friends kind feedback on their stories.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Can you guess what happened next? Today, Birimo is so excited that he can't sit still. He stands in front of the fire, holds up his notebook and reads his story to all of us. When he finishes, Granny Willa puts down her knitting and says, Now, my dears, a storyteller grows when friends give kind feedback. Here is my rule. First, say something you liked, and be specific. Then, give one gentle idea, not ten. Use Maybe you could, so it sounds friendly. Haru goes first. He says, I loved the part where the dragon sneezed. Maybe you could tell us more about the castle. Say it with me. I loved the part where the dragon sneezed. Maybe you could tell us more about the castle. Great! Birimo grins from ear to ear. Let's read the story that Birimo read to us. "The Dragon Who Sneezed Glitter, by Birimo. Fizz was a small green dragon who lived on a hill next to a big castle. Fizz had a problem. Whenever he smelled flowers, his nose began to tickle. Ah... ah... ACHOO! Instead of fire, a cloud of glitter came out! It flew across the sky like a shooting star and landed on everything. The queen's cat turned pink and sparkly. The guards' helmets turned gold and purple. Even the castle, which had been as white as snow, was now every color of the rainbow. Fizz felt terrible, so he hid behind a big rock. But the next morning, people came from far away to see the shining castle. The queen laughed and told Fizz, You're the best decorator in the kingdom!" What came out when Fizz sneezed? A cloud of glitter. Why did people come from far away? To see the shining castle. Kiko says, I loved the part where the cat turned pink. Riko adds, Maybe you could add a sound word for the glitter. Birimo nods. Thanks! That's a great idea. Granny Willa smiles. You see? Kind words first, then one idea. Now, phonics. Here are three more similes. The castle was as white as snow. Saffron's old scales are as hard as a rock. A simile can use like, too. The glitter flew like a shooting star. Which word goes in as white as ... ? Snow! Next time, we'll use our friends' ideas to rewrite our stories.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I loved the part where the dragon sneezed. Maybe you could tell us more about the castle. Today, Granny Willa gives each of us a fresh sheet of paper and a pencil. She says, The first draft is never the last draft, my dears. Even I rewrite my stories again and again. Then she shows us three tricks. One: change plain words into vivid words. Instead of said, try whispered, shouted or muttered. Two: add a simile, so the listener can see the picture. Three: cut extra words that don't help the story. Riko works on The Lighthouse Cat. When she finishes, she holds up her paper proudly and says, I changed 'said' to 'whispered.' Say it with me. I changed 'said' to 'whispered.' Great! She changed a lot of other things, too. Let's read the two versions of Riko's paragraph. "Before: The cat was in the lighthouse. It was night. There was a storm. A boat was coming. The cat was scared. She said, I have to help. She went up the stairs. She turned on the light. The boat was safe. After: On a stormy night, Pepper the lighthouse cat could not sleep. Far out at sea, a little fishing boat was rocking on the waves, and the lighthouse lamp had gone out! Her tail was shaking, but she whispered, I have to help. She ran like the wind up two hundred stairs and pushed the big switch with both paws. Click! The light swept across the water, as bright as the moon. Slowly, the little boat turned toward the harbor. That night, Pepper slept like a log." How did Riko show that Pepper was scared? Her tail was shaking. What did Pepper do to help the boat? She ran up the stairs and turned on the light. Haru says, Your new version is much better! It feels like a movie. Riko smiles. Thanks for your ideas. They really helped. Now, phonics. These similes use like. After a long, busy day, we sleep like a log. A good swimmer can swim like a fish. And Pepper ran like the wind. Which word goes in sleep like a ... ? Log! Next time, we'll tell our stories by the fire on Storytelling Night.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, I changed 'said' to 'whispered.' Tonight is Storytelling Night in the Hearth Room! Nib has put cushions and soft blankets all around the fire, and Granny Willa hands everyone a warm cup of cocoa. I sit with everyone in the firelight. Even Saffron, the old golden dragon, has come to listen. Each friend tells the beginning of a story. Riko tells The Lighthouse Cat, and Haru tells The Boy and the Stone Giant in a big, deep voice. Birimo tells The Dragon Who Sneezed Glitter, with a new sound word, whoosh! Then it's Kiko's turn. She takes a deep breath, pauses, and begins softly. Once, in a land beyond the clouds, there lived a girl who could talk to the wind. Say it with me. Once, in a land beyond the clouds, there lived a girl who could talk to the wind. Beautiful! Let's read the first page of Kiko's story. "Once, in a land beyond the clouds, there lived a girl who could talk to the wind. Her name was Aria. Every morning, the wind told her secrets: where the birds were flying, which flowers were opening, and when the rain was coming. Aria loved her village in the sky, with its cloud gardens and rainbow bridges. On the coldest night of the year, a strange wind knocked on her window. Its voice was soft and a little sad, and it was singing a song that Aria had never heard before. Come with me, it said. I'm lost, and I need a friend who can listen. Aria pulled on her warm coat and opened the window. The wind lifted her up, gently but quickly, over the edge of the clouds, toward a land she had never seen." Who is the hero of Kiko's story? A girl named Aria who can talk to the wind. Why did the strange wind come? Because it was lost and needed a friend. Everyone claps. Saffron's eyes shine. Then the Storybook starts to glow, and a fifth golden page appears! Nib reads it aloud. The fifth secret of stories: a story comes alive when you tell it aloud. Now, phonics. Let's review. He was as brave as a lion. After a long wait, finally, it was Kiko's turn. Out of the giant egg came, pause, a baby star. Leaves flutter in the wind. Next time, we'll read a longer tale about a grumpy king.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Once, in a land beyond the clouds, there lived a girl who could talk to the wind. Nib leads us to a quiet reading room full of soft chairs. On a tall stand, there is one thick book. Nib taps the cover with his feather pen and says, This tale is longer than the others, so read slowly. I ask one big question. Read the tale. Why did the king change his mind? Say it with me. Read the tale. Why did the king change his mind? Great! Let's read it together. "The King Who Banned Singing. Long ago, in a busy little town, there lived a king who was always grumpy. Every day, the town was full of noise. Bakers sang as they baked, children sang on their way to the market, and the bells rang every hour. The noise gave the king terrible headaches. So one morning, he made a new rule: No more singing! The town became very quiet, and very sad. Then one stormy night, thunder rolled across the sky. In her family's barn near the castle, a baby goat was so frightened that it couldn't stop crying. A little girl named Tess sat down beside it with her lantern and gently hummed a soft song. Slowly, the baby goat closed its eyes. Up in his tower, the king heard the song through his window. For the first time in years, he felt peaceful. The next morning, he changed the rule. Soft songs were allowed again, and from then on, the town had a singing day every year." Why did the king ban singing? Because the noise gave him headaches. Why did he change his mind? Because Tess's soft song made him feel peaceful for the first time in years. Kiko says, I think the king wasn't really bad. He was just tired. Riko says, I see your point, but he made the whole town sad. Nib claps his tiny paws. Good readers can disagree, as long as they give reasons! Now, phonics. Let's review. Glance means look very quickly. Sizzle is the sound of food in a hot pan. She had never seen the sea before, and now, pause, it was right in front of her. Tess gently hummed a song. The stormy night was as cold as ice. Next time, we'll hear a story told by a wolf.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, Read the tale. Why did the king change his mind? Today, Nib takes us down a path where the hedges are full of mirrors. In every mirror, we can see ourselves from a different side. Nib stops and says, Every story has more than one side, too. Most stories are told by the hero. But what about the other characters? Then he asks a question that makes us all think. What if the story were told by the wolf? Say it with me. What if the story were told by the wolf? Great! In many stories, the wolf is the bad guy. But maybe he has his own reasons. Let's read a story called The Lost Lamb, told by the wolf himself. "The Lost Lamb, Told by the Wolf. Everyone thinks I'm the bad guy in this story, but please listen. One foggy morning, I was out for a walk when I heard a tiny cry. A little lamb had wandered away from the farm and was stuck in a bush. When she saw me, she screamed. I have big teeth. But I only wanted to help! I pulled the branches apart carefully, and she ran off in the wrong direction, toward the river. I followed her, and every time she stopped, I gently pushed her toward the farm with my nose. When we finally arrived, the farmer saw me and shouted, Wolf! Everyone yelled and waved their arms, so I hurried back into the forest. Nobody believed me. But the lamb knows the truth. Last week, she left a basket of apples at my door with a note: Thank you." Why was the wolf following the lamb? Because he was trying to help her find her way home. How do we know the wolf is telling the truth? The lamb left him apples and a thank-you note. Haru says, From the wolf's point of view, he was a hero! Birimo adds, Poor wolf. I'm going to bake him a cake. Now, phonics. Let's review. Wander means walk slowly with no special place to go. Rustle is the sound of dry leaves. Little by little, the fog cleared, and they saw, pause, the castle. The lamb looked at the wolf curiously. A snowflake is as light as a feather. Next time, each of us will finish our final story.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, What if the story were told by the wolf? Today is a big day. Nib takes us to a sunny writing room with long wooden desks, colored pencils and stacks of clean paper. On each desk, there is a blank book cover. Nib says, Today, you finish your stories and make your covers. A story isn't finished until it has a title! I walk around the room and help everyone. Haru draws a huge stone giant with a gentle smile. Riko draws a cat on top of a lighthouse. Birimo decorates his cover with real glitter, and now his nose is sparkly, too. Kiko writes her title in curly blue letters, and then she reads it to us proudly. My story is called The Girl Who Talked to the Wind. Say it with me. My story is called The Girl Who Talked to the Wind. Wonderful! Let's read what Kiko wrote on the back cover of her book. "The Girl Who Talked to the Wind, by Kiko. Aria lives in a village above the clouds, and she can talk to the wind. On the coldest night of the year, a strange wind knocks on her window and carries her far away, to a land of dry deserts and tall mountains. Aria is lost and lonely. Just then, she hears a voice behind her. It's the youngest wind, and it is lost and lonely, too! Aria listens to its story and helps it find its way, and the two become good friends. In the end, the wind carries her home, and every night after that, a warm breeze sings outside her window. A story about friendship, courage and listening. For readers who love adventure and the sky." Whose voice does Aria hear behind her? The youngest wind's. How does Aria get home? The wind carries her home. Riko says, I love the last line. It feels so cozy. Kiko smiles. I'm proud of my ending. It's warm and happy. Now, phonics. Let's review. Kiko gives a big grin when she finishes. Drip is the sound of water falling one drop at a time. He reached into his pocket and pulled out, pause, a glowing stone. Kiko read her title proudly. After all that writing, tonight we'll sleep like a log. Next time, we'll take a goodbye tour of the Labyrinth.

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, My story is called The Girl Who Talked to the Wind. Today, Nib takes us on a goodbye tour of the Labyrinth. He holds the Storybook under his arm, and we walk past every room we have visited. We wave to the clever rabbit's room and the Moon Room. Saffron lifts her golden head from her pile of old books and says, Here's one last riddle for you. What has a beginning, a middle and an end, and lives inside you? A story! In the Hearth Room, Granny Willa gives each of us a warm hug. Then Riko says, I've learned so much here. If I were a storyteller, I would tell stories as bright as the stars. Say it with me. If I were a storyteller, I would tell stories as bright as the stars. Wonderful! Let's read Nib's map of our journey. "Our Journey Through the Labyrinth of Tales. In the first rooms, we heard tales from many lands: a clever rabbit, a moon that shares its light, and brave children everywhere. In Nib's Story Workshop, we learned about setting, characters and problems. We learned to show, not tell, and to use similes and sound words. In the Dragon Room and at the Well of Wishes, we imagined what we would do with magic. Then we planned our own stories, with strong beginnings, exciting turning points and happy endings. In the Hearth Room, Granny Willa taught us to tell stories aloud and to give kind feedback. Now our stories are finished, and the Storytelling Festival is waiting in the Central Hall!" Where did we learn about setting, characters and problems? In Nib's Story Workshop. Who taught us to tell stories aloud? Granny Willa. At the very end of the tour, we come to the exit of the maze. There is a round window in the wall. Through it, we can see rolling green hills under a soft sky, and the wind smells of flowers. Haru asks, What's that place? Nib smiles. That's the Highlands of the Heart. Now, phonics. Let's review. Stumble means almost fall while walking. Whoosh is the sound of something rushing past. The thing under the bed was not a monster, pause, but a puppy. Haru waited nervously for his turn. In the library, we were as quiet as a mouse. Next time, it's the Storytelling Festival!

lessons.teacherScript: Hello, everyone! Last time, we said, If I were a storyteller, I would tell stories as bright as the stars. Today is the Storytelling Festival! The Central Hall is at the very heart of the Labyrinth. It is round and tall, with shelves that go up and up, and thousands of tiny lanterns glimmer above us. Everyone is here. Granny Willa sits in the front row in her patchwork shawl. Saffron lies along the back wall, and the clever rabbit sits on her tail. I sit with everyone, and Nib stands on the stage in his red cape. Haru tells part of The Boy and the Stone Giant. Riko tells part of The Lighthouse Cat. Birimo tells The Dragon Who Sneezed Glitter, and everyone laughs. Kiko tells the end of her story, and the hall goes quiet. Then Nib says, Every one of us has a story to tell. Say it with me. Every one of us has a story to tell. Wonderful! Let's read the festival program. "The Storytelling Festival of the Labyrinth of Tales. Welcome to the Central Hall! Today, four young storytellers will share the stories they wrote here. Haru: The Boy and the Stone Giant, a tale about a lonely giant who learns to laugh. Riko: The Lighthouse Cat, a tale about a small cat with a big heart. Birimo: The Dragon Who Sneezed Glitter, a very funny tale. Please don't sit too close! Kiko: The Girl Who Talked to the Wind, a tale about friendship and listening. Please listen quietly, and cheer at the end of each story. When the last story is told, keep your eyes on the Storybook." Who tells the funny tale? Birimo. What should the audience do at the end of each story? Cheer. The cheers are loud and happy. Then the sixth golden page appears. The sixth secret of stories: every one of us has a story to tell. The Storybook is complete! It glows like a little sun. As Nib closes it, a pressed purple flower falls out with a note. It says, Come to the Highlands of the Heart. We remember the green hills from the window. Our next adventure is waiting! Now, phonics. Let's review. Lanterns glimmer in the dark. Old doors creak. The voice in the dark whispered one word, pause, welcome. Kiko told her story bravely. The idea came to her like a shooting star. Goodbye, Nib! Thank you, Granny Willa! Thank you, Labyrinth of Tales!

lines.speaker: Ms. Emma
lines.en: Welcome to the Storytelling Festival! Kiko, you're last. Please tell us your ending.
lines.ja: 物語フェスティバルへ ようこそ！ キコ、あなたが さいごよ。おわりの ところを 語って ね。

lines.speaker: Kiko
lines.en: Aria helped the youngest wind find its way, and they became friends...
lines.ja: アリアは いちばん 年下の 風が みちを 見つけるのを 手つだって、ふたりは 友だちに なりました…

lines.speaker: Birimo
lines.en: And then what happened?
lines.ja: それから どう なったの？

lines.speaker: Kiko
lines.en: The wind carried her home! And every night, a warm breeze sang outside her window.
lines.ja: 風が アリアを 家まで はこんだんだ！ それから まいばん、あたたかい そよ風が まどの 外で 歌ったの。

lines.speaker: Haru
lines.en: That ending gave me goosebumps. I think it's perfect, because the wind is her friend now, not a stranger.
lines.ja: その おわりかた、とりはだが 立ったよ。かんぺきだと 思う。風が もう 知らない ひとじゃ なくて 友だちに なったから。

lines.speaker: Riko
lines.en: Look! The sixth golden page! The Storybook is complete!
lines.ja: 見て！ 6まいめの 金の ページ！ 物語の 本が かんせいした！

lines.speaker: Kiko
lines.en: Every one of us has a story to tell.
lines.ja: わたしたち ひとり ひとりに、語る お話が あるんだ。

lines.speaker: Birimo
lines.en: Look! A purple flower!
lines.ja: 見て！ むらさきの 花！

lines.speaker: Haru
lines.en: There's a note with it! It says, Come to the Highlands of the Heart.
lines.ja: 手紙も ついてる！「こころの高原へ おいで」って 書いて ある。

lines.speaker: Ms. Emma
lines.en: The green hills from the window! I wonder whose heart is waiting there.
lines.ja: まどから 見えた みどりの 丘ね！ あそこで だれの こころが まって いるのかしら。

aiTask.goalJa: AI の ニブが 物語フェスティバルの 司会を するよ。自分の 物語の 一部を 語って、Every one of us has a story to tell. で しめくくろう。ニブが「And then what happened?」と きいたら つづきを 話そう。ニブが「What was your favorite part of the Labyrinth? Why?」と きいたら りゆうも いおう。6 かい いじょう やりとり しよう
